full_judgment:
The preempted is the petitioner in this Rule obtained u/s. 115 (old) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Miscellaneous application of the pre-emptor opposite party No. 1 was allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Mymensingh and on appeal the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Mymensingh upheld the judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge and dismissed the appeal. Mr Abdul Hamid, learned Advocate for the preempted petitioner has raised a new point which was not raised in the two Courts below. He submits that the pre-emptor opposite party No. 1 nowhere stated in his miscellaneous application that he is a person to whom transfer of the case land can be made u/s. 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In the absence of any such averment in the miscellaneous application the preempted petitioner also did not say anything in the matter. No evidence was led by either party on this issue, nor any issue was framed on the subject. None of the two courts below has given any finding that the pre-emptor opposite party No. 1 holds land as permissible u/s. 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 5. The learned Additional District Judge seems to have overlooked the fact that the splitting up of the jama was effected by the concerned Revenue Officer u/s. 117 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act. The first proviso to section 117 requires that the Revenue Officer shall pass no order of sub-division unless reasonable notice is given to the parties concerned to appear and be beard in the matter. From Ext. C the certified copy of the order dated 10-2-70 it appears that notices were served upon the co-sharer tenants by the Tahsilder and no objection appears to have been filed. 

 6. The learned Additional District Judge finds that there is no evidence to show that all the co-sharers were served with notices in the present case. Obviously he means to say that the provisions of section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act have not been followed. Under the Bengal Tenancy Act a division of a tenancy was not valid unless consented to by all the parties or ordered by a Civil Court. By an amendment to the B. T. Act in 1958 namely, Bengal Tenancy (East Pakistan 3rd Amendment) Ordinance, 1958 section 88A was added to the B.T. Act. Power was given to the Revenue Officer to affect division of 'the holding. In the case of Kafizan Bibi, vs. Hazi Farid Kazi, 18 DLR 281 it was held that all rent-receiving interests in the province stood acquired and the Provincial Government became the sole landlord in respect of the holding in question. That being so, the Revenue Officer was fully competent under sub-section (1) of the newly added section 88A to effect the disputed sub-division. 

 7. Section 117 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act also empowers the Revenue Officer to effect sub-division of a holding. The one requirement is that he will give reasonable notice to the parties concerned to appear and be heard in the matter. In the present case the Revenue Officer has effected a sub-division after serving notice upon the co-sharer tenants and having received no objection thereto, the sub-division is therefore complete. The subject matter of the disputed transfer thereafter appertained to a. sub-divided jama in which the pre-emptor opposite party No. 1 ceased to be a co-sharer. He ceased to be a co-sharer of the petitioner's vendor in respect of the junta with effect from 10-2-70. As such he has no locus standi to come u/s. 96 and seek pre-emption in respect of the disputed transfer. I, therefore, hold that the two courts below acted illegally and with material irregularity in allowing pre-emption in the present case.
